article.title: What Do Whales Feel?
glossary: * Echolocation: the perception of objects by means of sound wave echoes.

items.sentence_raw: Some of the senses that we and other terrestrial mammals take for granted are either reduced or absent in cetaceans or fail to function well in water.
For example, it appears from their brain structure that toothed species are unable to smell.
Baleen species, on the other hand, appear to have some related brain structures but it is not known whether these are functional.
It has been speculated that, as the blowholes evolved and migrated to the top of the head, the neural pathways serving sense of smell may have been nearly all sacrificed.
Similarly, although at least some cetaceans have taste buds, the nerves serving these have degenerated or are rudimentary.
items.explain: Q15: The passage says *'the nerves serving these have degenerated or are rudimentary'* — **'these'** refers to **'taste buds'** mentioned just before. **'Degenerated'** and **'rudimentary'** both mean **'underdeveloped'**. So the answer is **taste buds**.

items.sentence_raw: The sense of touch has sometimes been described as weak too, but this view is probably mistaken.

Trainers of captive dolphins and small whales often remark on their animals' responsiveness to being touched or rubbed, and both captive and free-ranging cetacean individuals of all species (particularly adults and calves, or members of the same subgroup) appear to make frequent contact.
This contact may help to maintain order within a group, and stroking or touching are part of the courtship ritual in most species.
items.explain: Q22: The passage says *'stroking or touching are part of the courtship ritual'* — **'courtship ritual'** means **'mating'**. The question asks which sense is involved in mating. So the answer is **touch**.

items.sentence_raw: The area around the blowhole is also particularly sensitive and captive animals often object strongly to being touched there.
The sense of vision is developed to different degrees in different species.

Baleen species studied at close quarters underwater - specifically a grey whale calf in captivity for a year, and free-ranging right whales and humpback whales studied and filmed off Argentina and Hawaii - have obviously tracked objects with vision underwater, and they can apparently see moderately well both in water and in air.
However, the position of the eyes so restricts the field of vision in baleen whales that they probably do not have stereoscopic vision.
items.explain: Q16: The passage directly states *'the position of the eyes so restricts the field of vision in baleen whales that they probably do not have stereoscopic vision'*. The question asks which species lacks this ability. So the answer is **baleen whales**.

items.sentence_raw: On the other hand, the position of the eyes in most dolphins and porpoises suggests that they have stereoscopic vision forward and downward.
items.explain: Q17: The passage says dolphins and porpoises *'have stereoscopic vision forward and downward'*. The question asks for the two directions of their vision. So the answers are **forward** and **downward**.

items.sentence_raw: Eye position in freshwater dolphins, which often swim on their side or upside down while feeding, suggests that what vision they have is stereoscopic forward and upward.
items.explain:
Q18: The passage mentions *'freshwater dolphins, which often swim on their side or upside down while feeding'*. The question asks which species swims upside down. So the answer is **freshwater dolphins**.

Q23: The passage mentions *'freshwater dolphins, which often swim on their side or upside down while feeding'*. The question asks which species swims upside down while eating. So the answer is **freshwater dolphins**.

items.sentence_raw: By comparison, the bottlenose dolphin has extremely keen vision in water.
items.explain: Q19: The passage says the bottlenose dolphin has *'extremely keen vision in water'* — **'extremely keen'** means **'exceptional'**. The question asks where their vision is exceptional. So the answer is **water**.

items.sentence_raw: Judging from the way it watches and tracks airborne flying fish, it can apparently see fairly well through the air-water interface as well.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says the bottlenose dolphin *'watches and tracks airborne flying fish'* — **'tracks'** means **'follows'**. The question asks what they can follow from under the water. So the answer is **flying fish**.

items.sentence_raw: And although preliminary experimental evidence suggests that their in-air vision is poor, the accuracy with which dolphins leap high to take small fish out of a trainer's hand provides anecdotal evidence to the contrary.
Such variation can no doubt be explained with reference to the habitats in which individual species have developed.
For example, vision is obviously more useful to species inhabiting clear open waters than to those living in turbid rivers and flooded plains.
items.explain: Q25: The passage explains vision is *'more useful to species inhabiting clear open waters'* — **'inhabiting'** means **'living in'**, and **'more useful'** means **'related to good visual ability'**. The question asks which habitat is related to good vision. So the answer is **clear open waters**.

items.sentence_raw: The South American boutu and Chinese beiji, for instance, appear to have very limited vision, and the Indian susus are blind, their eyes reduced to slits that probably allow them to sense only the direction and intensity of light.

Although the senses of taste and smell appear to have deteriorated, and vision in water appears to be uncertain, such weaknesses are more than compensated for by cetaceans' well-developed acoustic sense.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says weaknesses in other senses *'are more than compensated for by cetaceans' well-developed acoustic sense'* — **'well-developed'** means **'best developed'**. The question asks which sense is best developed. So the answer is **acoustic sense**.

items.sentence_raw: Most species are highly vocal, although they vary in the range of sounds they produce, and many forage for food using echo-location*.
Large baleen whales primarily use the lower frequencies and are often limited in their repertoire.
items.explain: Q20: The passage states large baleen whales *'primarily use the lower frequencies'*. The question asks what type of sound they usually use. So the answer is **lower frequencies**.

items.sentence_raw: Notable exceptions are the nearly song-like choruses of bowhead whales in summer and the complex, haunting utterances of the humpback whales.
items.explain: Q21: The passage gives *'notable exceptions'* as *'bowhead whales'* and *'humpback whales'*, describing their sounds as *'song-like'*. The question asks which two species have song-like sounds. So the answers are **bowhead** and **humpback**.

items.sentence_raw: Toothed species in general employ more of the frequency spectrum, and produce a wider variety of sounds, than baleen species (though the sperm whale apparently produces a monotonous series of high-energy clicks and little else).

Some of the more complicated sounds are clearly communicative, although what role they may play in the social life and 'culture' of cetaceans has been more the subject of wild speculation than of solid science.

subtitles: An examination of the functioning of the senses in cetaceans, the group of mammals comprising whales, dolphins and porpoises
